source.title: Early Lives of Charlemagne
source.attribution: Einhard and Notker the Stammerer, Early Lives of Charlemagne (trans. A. J. Grant), Project Gutenberg, public domain
source.notes: Einhard's Life (written about 817-830) and the Monk of St Gall's anecdotes (about 883), in A. J. Grant's translation (first published 1905; Grant died 1948): public domain in the US and in life+70 countries. Locators use the translation's spelling 'Eginhard'.

cards.title: Trust the witness who also tells you what he doesn't know
cards.body:
Einhard grew up at Charlemagne's court in what is now Aachen, in western Germany, and wrote his Life of the king some years after Charles died in 814. He gave two reasons: he had seen most of the events himself, and he owed the king a debt of friendship.

What makes him worth trusting is a small admission. He says he will write nothing about Charles's birth and boyhood, because he found nothing written down and nobody alive who remembered. Rather than invent a childhood, he left a gap.

When you read any account of a famous person, look for that kind of honesty. A writer who marks the edges of their knowledge is usually more reliable inside those edges.
cards.quote: for I knew that no one could write of these events more truthfully than I could, since I was myself an actor in them, and, being present, knew them from the testimony of my own eyes
cards.locator: The Life of the Emperor Charles. Written by Eginhard ¶2
cards.apply_it: Next time you read a confident claim online, ask: how does this writer know, and do they say what they don't know?

quiz.question: Why did Einhard skip Charlemagne's childhood?
options: He found no records and no living witnesses
Charles asked him to keep it secret
quiz.explanation: He refused to invent what he could not check, which is part of why historians value his account.

cards.title: A crown without power is only a costume
cards.body:
Before Charlemagne's family took the throne, the Franks, who ruled much of what is now France and western Germany, still had kings from the old Merovingian line. By the 700s those kings had nothing left but the title. Einhard describes the last of them sitting on the throne with long hair and beard, repeating answers to ambassadors that others had written for him, and riding to assemblies in an ox cart.

Real power sat with the Mayors of the Palace, Charlemagne's grandfather and father among them. In 751 the last Merovingian was deposed and sent to a monastery.

In any organisation, look past job titles. The person who controls the money and the decisions is the one actually in charge.
cards.quote: For the wealth and power of the kingdom was in the hands of the Praefects of the Court, who were called Mayors of the Palace, and exercised entire sovereignty.
cards.locator: The Life of the Emperor Charles. Written by Eginhard ¶6
cards.apply_it: Think of a group you belong to. Who holds the title, and who actually makes the decisions? Are they the same person?

quiz.question: Who really ran the Frankish kingdom before Charlemagne's father became king?
quiz.explanation: The Merovingian kings kept the title, but the Mayors of the Palace held the wealth and made the decisions.

cards.title: Charlemagne inherited a kingdom his grandfather and father had fought to build
cards.body:
Charlemagne's grandfather, Charles Martel ('the Hammer'), defeated an invading army from Muslim Spain near Poitiers, in west-central France, in 732, and won again near Narbonne in the south. His son Pippin, Charlemagne's father, went further: in 751 he was made king in place of the powerless Merovingian, with the approval of the Pope, and ruled until his death in 768.

So when the young Charles came to the throne, he did not start from nothing. Three generations of hard work had already made his family the strongest in western Europe.

Behind most 'self-made' success there is usually a foundation someone else laid. Knowing what you inherited helps you judge your own part fairly.
cards.quote: But Pippin, after he was made King instead of Mayor of the Palace by the authority of the Roman Pontiff, exercised sole rule over the Franks for fifteen years, or rather more.
cards.locator: The Life of the Emperor Charles. Written by Eginhard ¶9
cards.apply_it: Name one advantage you started with that you did not earn yourself. How might you pass something similar on?

quiz.question: Who won the battle near Poitiers in 732?
quiz.explanation: Charles Martel, Charlemagne's grandfather, turned back the invading army near Poitiers in 732.

cards.title: He shared the kingdom with a difficult brother and refused to be provoked
cards.body:
When Pippin died in 768, the Frankish custom was to split the kingdom between sons. Charles and his younger brother Carloman each received a share. Their partnership was tense: Carloman's supporters tried to drive the brothers apart, and some hoped for war between them.

Einhard says Charles put up with his brother's quarrelling so patiently that he never lost his temper with him. Carloman died of illness in 771, and Charles became sole king with the agreement of the Frankish nobles. A civil war that could have wrecked the kingdom never happened.

Patience with a difficult partner is not weakness. Sometimes refusing to take the bait is what keeps the whole thing standing.
cards.quote: As long as, after the death of his father, he shared the kingdom with his brother he bore so patiently the quarrelling and restlessness of the latter as never even to be provoked to wrath by him.
cards.locator: Part II. Private Life and Character of Charlemagne ¶2
cards.apply_it: Who is the person most likely to provoke you this week? Decide in advance one response that keeps the peace.

quiz.question: How did Charles handle his brother Carloman's quarrelling, according to Einhard?
options: He went to war with him
He asked the Pope to judge between them
He bore it patiently and never lost his temper
quiz.explanation: Einhard says Charles was never provoked to anger by his brother, and the kingdom avoided civil war.

cards.title: His first war was one his father had left unfinished, and he saw it through
cards.body:
Charles's first campaign, in 769, was in Aquitaine, in south-western France, where his father had fought for nine years without quite finishing. A rebel named Hunold had tried to revive the revolt. Charles asked his brother for help; Carloman promised it and then did not come.

Charles carried on anyway. He chased Hunold across the Garonne river into Gascony and told the local duke to hand him over or face war. The duke gave up Hunold and submitted.

Unfinished work has a way of coming back. Einhard's point is simple: Charles did not slow down until the job was actually done, even when the help he was promised never arrived.
cards.quote: would not desist or slacken in his task before, by perseverance and continuous effort, he had completely reached the end after which he strove
cards.locator: Part I. His Exploits at Home and Abroad ¶1
cards.apply_it: Pick one task you have left 90 percent finished. What is the single step that would close it today?

quiz.question: What happened when Charles asked his brother for help in Aquitaine?
options: Carloman promised help but did not provide it
quiz.explanation: Carloman failed to send the help he promised, but Charles finished the campaign anyway.

cards.title: Where his father settled for a promise, Charles took the whole kingdom
cards.body:
In 773, answering an appeal from Pope Hadrian, Charles led his army over the Alps against Desiderius, king of the Lombards in northern Italy. His father had fought the Lombards before but accepted hostages and a promise, which was soon broken.

Charles did not stop at a promise. He besieged Pavia, near modern Milan, until Desiderius surrendered in 774, sent the Lombard king into permanent exile, drove out his son, and made himself king of the Lombards. Later he set his own son Pippin over Italy.

The story shows a pattern in his reign: he preferred final settlements to temporary ones. Whether that is wise depends on the cost, and in Italy it meant the end of an independent kingdom.
cards.quote: But King Charles, when once he had begun the war, did not stop until he had received the surrender of King Desiderius, whom he had worn down after a long siege
cards.locator: Part I. His Exploits at Home and Abroad ¶2
cards.apply_it: Is there a problem you keep patching with promises? What would a lasting fix look like, and what would it cost?

quiz.question: How did Charles's Lombard war differ from his father's?
options: He kept going until the Lombard king surrendered and Italy was his
He refused to go to Italy
He let the Pope fight it
quiz.explanation: Pippin accepted hostages and a promise; Charles besieged Pavia until Desiderius surrendered and took over the kingdom.

cards.title: The longest war of his reign began with raids on an open border
cards.body:
The Saxons lived in what is now northern Germany, between the Rhine and the Elbe. They kept their own gods and their independence. Einhard explains that the Frankish and Saxon lands met across open plains with few natural boundaries, so raids, killings and burnings happened constantly on both sides.

The Franks eventually decided retaliation was not enough and went to war. It began in 772 and, with breaks, lasted more than thirty years, until about 804. Einhard calls it the longest and cruellest war the Franks ever fought.

Long conflicts often grow from small, repeated injuries that nobody stops. The cheapest time to settle a dispute is usually early, before both sides have a list of grievances.
cards.quote: Never was there a war more prolonged nor more cruel than this, nor one that required greater efforts on the part of the Frankish peoples.
cards.locator: Part I. His Exploits at Home and Abroad ¶3
cards.apply_it: Is there a small, repeated friction in your life that could grow into something bigger? What would settling it early look like?

quiz.question: According to Einhard, what kept causing trouble between Franks and Saxons?
options: A dispute over a royal marriage
An open border where raids happened constantly on both sides
quiz.explanation: With few natural barriers between them, murder, robbery and arson were constant on both sides of the border.

cards.title: Charlemagne made the Saxons choose between baptism and death
cards.body:
Einhard presents the end of the Saxon war as a settlement: the Saxons would give up their old religion, accept Christian baptism and become one people with the Franks. He also records that Charles removed ten thousand people, with their wives and children, from both banks of the Elbe and resettled them across Germany and Gaul.

The book's editor is blunter. He writes that the conversion was forced, with death or baptism set before the Saxons, and that later writers took it for granted that argument alone could not change a people's faith.

Faith imposed by the sword is not the same as faith freely chosen. A fair history names the cost as well as the outcome, whoever is telling the story.
cards.quote: he took ten thousand of the inhabitants of both banks of the Elbe, with their wives and children, and planted them in many groups in various parts of Germany and Gaul.
cards.locator: Part I. His Exploits at Home and Abroad ¶5
cards.apply_it: Think of a belief you hold deeply. How did you come to it, and how would you feel if someone tried to force a different one on you?

quiz.question: What does the editor's note say about how Saxony became Christian?
options: It was forced, with death or baptism set before the Saxons
The Saxons asked to be converted
quiz.explanation: The editor notes the conversion was of 'the most forcible kind': the Saxons were given a choice between death and baptism.

cards.title: Einhard blamed the queen for the king's cruelty, but the dates don't fit
cards.body:
In 782, at Verden in northern Germany, Charles ordered the killing of about 4,500 Saxon prisoners after a rebellion. Einhard never mentions it. Elsewhere he suggests that the harsh episodes of the reign came from the influence of Queen Fastrada, who, he says, turned Charles away from his natural kindness.

The editor points out the problem: the worst act of the reign, the massacre of the Saxons, happened before Charles married Fastrada.

Admiring biographers often find someone else to blame for their hero's worst deeds. The same instinct appears in families, workplaces and politics. When a person we admire does harm, the honest response is to let the responsibility land where it belongs.
cards.quote: Dr Hodgkin, however, points out that the most cruel act of his reign--the massacre of 4500 Saxons--took place before his marriage with Fastrada.
cards.locator: Notes ¶40
cards.apply_it: Think of someone you admire. Can you name one thing they did wrong without explaining it away?

quiz.question: Why does the editor doubt Einhard's claim that Fastrada caused the king's cruelty?
options: The massacre of the Saxons happened before Charles married her
quiz.explanation: The massacre at Verden in 782 came before the marriage, so it cannot be blamed on Fastrada's influence.

cards.title: He fought only two battles in person in a thirty-year war
cards.body:
For all its length, Charles himself met the Saxons in open battle only twice, both within a single month in 783, near Detmold and at the river Hase near Osnabrück. The rest of the fighting he left to his counts.

His war against the Avars, in what is now Hungary, followed the same pattern. He led one expedition in person and handed the rest to his son Pippin, his governors and his officers, who finished it after eight years.

The great warrior king was, in practice, a great delegator. He kept the strategy and trusted others with the execution. Anyone leading a team faces the same choice: be everywhere, or build people who can act without you.
cards.quote: In this war, despite its prolongation through so many years, he did not himself meet the enemy in battle more than twice
cards.locator: Part I. His Exploits at Home and Abroad ¶6
cards.apply_it: Which task do you still do yourself that someone on your team could own? Hand over one piece of it this week.

quiz.question: How often did Charles personally fight the Saxons in open battle, according to Einhard?
quiz.explanation: He fought only two battles in person, both in one month; his counts and officers did the rest.

cards.title: Neither broken by bad news nor fooled by good news
cards.body:
While the Saxon war dragged on, Charles was also fighting in Italy, Spain, Bavaria and the east. Einhard marvels that no enterprise was dropped anywhere, and wonders whether his endurance or his luck deserves more credit.

His answer is a quality of mind. Charles, he says, understood the true nature of each task, so setbacks did not crush him and success did not flatter him into carelessness.

This is a useful test for anyone carrying a lot at once. A bad week is not the end, and a good week is not proof you can stop paying attention. Seeing a task clearly, for what it really is, is what keeps you steady in both.
cards.quote: He understood the true character of each task that he undertook or carried through, and thus was neither broken by adversity nor misled by the false flatteries of good fortune.
cards.locator: Part I. His Exploits at Home and Abroad ¶7
cards.apply_it: After your next win or setback, write one sentence describing the situation as it really is, without the mood.

quiz.question: What did Einhard say kept Charles steady through so many wars?
options: Understanding the true character of each task
quiz.explanation: Because he saw each task clearly, adversity did not break him and success did not mislead him.

cards.title: Roncevaux: a rearguard ambush that became Europe's favourite legend
cards.body:
In 778 Charles crossed the Pyrenees into Spain with a large army and took the towns he attacked. On the way home, in the mountain passes near Roncevaux, in what is now Navarre in northern Spain, local mountain fighters (Einhard calls them Gascons; historians usually say Basques) ambushed the rearguard and baggage train from the wooded heights. They killed every man in it and vanished into the night. Among the dead was Roland, warden of the Breton frontier.

The editor notes this is the only place the historical Roland appears. Later poets turned him into a legendary hero, the Roland of the Song of Roland.

A small, painful defeat can outlive a hundred victories in memory. Stories, not statistics, decide what people remember.
cards.quote: In this battle Eggihard, the surveyor of the royal table; Anselm, the Count of the Palace; and Roland, Praefect of the Breton frontier, were killed along with very many others.
cards.locator: Part I. His Exploits at Home and Abroad ¶8
cards.apply_it: Which story about your family or workplace gets retold most? Is it a triumph or a setback, and why do you think it stuck?

quiz.question: What happened at Roncevaux in 778?
options: Mountain fighters ambushed and wiped out the Frankish rearguard
quiz.explanation: The rearguard was ambushed in the Pyrenees passes and killed to the last man; Roland was among the dead.

cards.title: He let a stubborn duke keep his pride because the people mattered more
cards.body:
In 787 Charles marched into southern Italy and camped at Capua, threatening the Duchy of Benevento. Duke Aragis sent his two sons as hostages with a large sum of money and promised obedience, with one odd condition: he would not come to meet the king in person.

Charles could have forced the point. Instead, Einhard says, he weighed what was good for the people of Benevento above the duke's obstinacy. He accepted the terms, kept only the younger son as hostage and sent the elder home to his father.

Winning the substance and letting the other side keep face is often the better deal. Insisting on every symbolic point can turn a settled dispute into a war.
cards.quote: Charles, considering rather the advantage of the people than their Duke's obstinacy, received the hostages who were offered him, and as a great favour consented to forego a personal interview.
cards.locator: Part I. His Exploits at Home and Abroad ¶10
cards.apply_it: In a current disagreement, is there a symbolic point you could let go if you get what really matters?

quiz.question: Why did Charles accept Duke Aragis's refusal to meet him in person?
options: He put the good of the people above the duke's stubbornness
He was afraid of the duke
He was too ill to travel
quiz.explanation: Einhard says Charles considered the people's advantage rather than the duke's obstinacy, and avoided a war.

cards.title: The Avar war brought the Franks treasure and left a land empty
cards.body:
From 791 Charles's armies fought the Avars, a powerful people based in Pannonia, the plain of modern Hungary. The war lasted eight years. The Avars' ruling class was destroyed, and the great treasure they had gathered over generations was carried back to the Franks, who, Einhard says, had until then been thought a poor people.

Einhard is honest about the cost. Pannonia, he writes, was left deserted, and where the Avar ruler's palace stood there was no trace of human life. The editor adds that the flood of gold raised prices across the Frankish lands.

Victory is rarely as clean as the treasure suggests. Someone always pays, and the bill often arrives in places the victors never see.
cards.quote: How many battles were fought there and how much blood was shed is still shown by the deserted and uninhabited condition of Pannonia
cards.locator: Part I. His Exploits at Home and Abroad ¶13
cards.apply_it: Think of a recent 'win' you had. Who else paid part of the price for it?

quiz.question: What evidence of the Avar war's cost does Einhard point to?
quiz.explanation: Einhard says the empty, uninhabited state of Pannonia still showed how much blood had been shed.

cards.title: A Christian king and a Muslim caliph traded gifts, including an elephant
cards.body:
Charles kept up friendly relations with Harun al-Rashid, the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad, whom Einhard calls 'Aaron, King of the Persians'. When Charles's envoys went with gifts to the holy places in Jerusalem, Harun granted their requests, sent his own ambassadors back with them and loaded them with robes, spices and other goods from the East. Earlier he had sent Charles an elephant, which reached Aachen in 802 and caused a sensation across Europe.

The editor notes how odd it is that later legend turned Charles into a crusader against Muslims, when the real man worked hard to keep this friendship.

Good relations across deep differences take effort and generosity, and they are often forgotten by later storytellers who prefer conflict.
cards.quote: a few years earlier he had sent him at his request an elephant,[36] which was then the only one he had.
cards.locator: Part I. His Exploits at Home and Abroad ¶20
cards.apply_it: Is there someone very different from you whose goodwill would help both of you? What small gesture could start it?

quiz.question: What famous gift did Harun al-Rashid send Charlemagne?
quiz.explanation: Harun sent Charles an elephant at his request, along with robes, spices and other riches.

cards.title: He built ships and coastal forts before the Viking raids grew
cards.body:
Late in his reign, raiders from Denmark and Scandinavia began attacking the coasts of Gaul and Germany. Their king, Godfred, boasted he would march on Aachen; he was killed by one of his own men in 810 before he could try.

Charles did not wait for luck. He built a fleet on the rivers flowing to the North Sea and put forts and garrisons in every harbour and river mouth. He did the same along the Mediterranean coasts against raiders from North Africa. Einhard says that, apart from a few places, the coasts suffered no serious harm in his time.

The best defences are the ones built before the crisis is obvious. Preparation is quiet work that only looks wise afterwards.
cards.quote: he planted forts and garrisons in all harbours and at the mouths of all navigable rivers, and prevented in this way the passage of the enemy.
cards.locator: Part I. His Exploits at Home and Abroad ¶23
cards.apply_it: What is one risk you can see coming? Take one small preparatory step this week, before it arrives.

quiz.question: How did Charles defend his coasts against the Northmen?
options: He paid them to stay away
He built a fleet and placed forts and garrisons at harbours and river mouths
He did nothing and relied on luck
quiz.explanation: He built ships and fortified harbours and river mouths, and the coasts suffered little harm in his day.

cards.title: He built great works, and he also ordered the old ones repaired
cards.body:
Between wars, Charles built. His two greatest works, Einhard says, were the church of St Mary at Aachen, which still stands as part of Aachen Cathedral, and a 500-foot wooden bridge over the Rhine at Mainz. He also began palaces at Ingelheim, near Mainz, and at Nijmegen, in what is now the Netherlands.

Just as important was a less glamorous order: bishops and priests across the realm were to restore any church that had fallen into ruin with age, and his agents were to check that it was done.

New projects get the attention, but maintenance keeps a place alive. Whether in a city, a business or a home, someone has to care for what already exists.
cards.quote: And he gave special orders to the bishops and priests who had charge of sacred buildings that any throughout his realm which had fallen into ruin through age should be restored, and he instructed his agents to see that his orders were carried out.
cards.locator: Part I. His Exploits at Home and Abroad ¶22
cards.apply_it: Choose one thing you own or look after that has been quietly falling apart, and fix or tidy it today.

quiz.question: Besides new buildings, what did Charles order across his realm?
options: That all old churches be torn down
That ruined churches be restored, with agents checking the work
That no new churches be built
That bridges be made of gold
quiz.explanation: He ordered decayed churches restored and sent agents to make sure it happened.

cards.title: Crowned emperor on Christmas Day 800, he said he would have stayed away
cards.body:
In 799 Pope Leo III was attacked by enemies in Rome and fled to Charles for protection. Charles came to Rome to restore order and spent the winter there. On Christmas Day 800, in St Peter's, the Pope crowned him Emperor and Augustus, reviving the title in the West for the first time in over three hundred years.

Einhard says Charles disliked it so much at first that he would not have entered the church that day had he known. The editor suggests the objection was to the manner: the crown seemed to come as the Pope's gift rather than from Charles's own power, which later fed centuries of conflict between popes and emperors.

How an honour is given can matter as much as the honour itself.
cards.quote: It was then that he received the title of Emperor and Augustus,[48] which he so disliked at first that he affirmed that he would not have entered the church on that day
cards.locator: Part II. Private Life and Character of Charlemagne ¶23
cards.apply_it: Before accepting a favour or title, ask what strings or expectations come with the way it is offered.

quiz.question: What does the editor think Charles most likely disliked about his coronation?
options: That the crown seemed to come as a gift from the Pope
That it happened on Christmas Day
quiz.explanation: The editor suggests he objected to the method: the title looked like the Pope's to give, which later caused long conflict.

cards.title: He answered a rival's anger by calling them brothers
cards.body:
The emperors in Constantinople saw themselves as the only true Roman emperors, and they were furious when Charles took the title in 800. They suspected he wanted their empire.

Einhard says Charles bore their hostility very calmly. He sent embassy after embassy, addressed the eastern emperors as his brothers, and in the end a treaty settled the quarrel. Einhard also records a Greek proverb of the time, 'the Frank is a good friend but a bad neighbour', which shows how much patience the job needed.

When someone resents your success, matching their anger rarely helps. Generosity and steady, repeated contact can wear down suspicion that arguments never would.
cards.quote: He conquered their ill-feeling by his magnanimity, in which, doubtless, he far excelled them, and sent frequent embassies to them, and called them his brothers.
cards.locator: Part II. Private Life and Character of Charlemagne ¶23
cards.apply_it: Is someone resentful of you right now? Send them one generous, no-strings message this week.

quiz.question: How did Charles respond to the eastern emperors' anger at his new title?
options: He sent frequent embassies and called them brothers
quiz.explanation: He overcame their ill-feeling with magnanimity, frequent embassies and brotherly language, and a treaty followed.

cards.title: He had the laws, songs and month names of his people written down
cards.body:
After 800, Charles noticed that the Franks lived under two different law codes. He planned to reconcile them but finished little. He did, however, order the unwritten laws of every people in his empire to be collected and written down.

He also had the old songs about the deeds and wars of earlier kings written out, began a grammar of his own Germanic language, and gave the months native names such as Hay-month for July and Harvest-month for August.

The editor adds a sad footnote: the collection of songs is lost, partly because his son Louis disliked the old poems. What is not written down and cared for can vanish within one generation.
cards.quote: He also wrote out the barbarous and ancient songs, in which the acts of the kings and their wars were sung, and committed them to memory. He also began a grammar of his native language.
cards.locator: Part II. Private Life and Character of Charlemagne ¶25
cards.apply_it: Record one family story, recipe or saying from an older relative this month, before it is lost.

quiz.question: What happened to the old songs Charles had collected?
options: They became the Song of Roland
They are kept in Aachen today
They were lost, partly because his son disliked them
quiz.explanation: The editor notes the collection disappeared, partly because Louis the Pious rejected the old poems.

cards.title: He gave his daughters the same schooling as his sons
cards.body:
Charles made sure all his children, daughters as well as sons, studied the liberal arts that he valued so much himself. That was unusual for the time. His sons also learned to ride, use weapons and hunt in the Frankish way, and his daughters learned wool-working, which Einhard says was meant to keep them from idleness and to build good character.

The practical training followed the customs of the age, but the core decision stands out: learning was not kept for the boys.

Whatever your children's interests, giving every one of them the same chance at a real education is one of the most lasting gifts a parent can make.
cards.quote: In educating his children he determined to train them, both sons and daughters, in those liberal studies to which he himself paid great attention.
cards.locator: Part II. Private Life and Character of Charlemagne ¶5
cards.apply_it: Is there a subject or skill you assume only one of your children (or one kind of child) needs? Offer it to all of them.

quiz.question: Which of his children did Charles have taught the liberal arts?
options: Both his sons and his daughters
quiz.explanation: Einhard says he trained both sons and daughters in the liberal studies he himself cared about.

cards.title: He never ate a meal at home without his children
cards.body:
For a man who ruled most of western Europe, Charles was remarkably present at home. Einhard says that when he was home he never dined without his children, and he never travelled without them: his sons rode beside him and his daughters followed, with guards set to watch over them.

When his son Pippin, king of Italy, died in 810, Charles made Pippin's young son Bernard king in his place and brought Pippin's five daughters to be raised alongside his own.

Busy parents often believe that presence must wait until things calm down. Charles shows another way: build the children into the daily routine itself, at the table and on the road.
cards.quote: He had such care of the upbringing of his sons and daughters that he never dined without them when he was at home, and never travelled without them.
cards.locator: Part II. Private Life and Character of Charlemagne ¶8
cards.apply_it: Choose one regular meal this week that the whole family eats together, phones away.

quiz.question: What did Charles do for his son Pippin's children after Pippin died?
options: Made Bernard king and raised the girls with his own daughters
Left them in Italy without support
Gave them to the Pope to raise
quiz.explanation: He appointed his grandson Bernard to succeed Pippin and brought up his granddaughters with his own daughters.

cards.title: He loved his daughters too much to let them go, and it cost them
cards.body:
Einhard is frank about one failure in Charles's family life. He loved his daughters so much that he refused to let any of them marry, at home or abroad, saying he could not do without their company. He kept them all at court until he died.

The result, Einhard admits, was scandal and failure in the one area where his good fortune broke down. Charles shut his eyes to it and acted as if he had heard nothing.

Love that will not let go can hold adult children back. Part of a parent's care is helping children build lives of their own, even when it means seeing less of them.
cards.quote: But up to his death he kept them all at home, saying that he could not forego their society.
cards.locator: Part II. Private Life and Character of Charlemagne ¶8
cards.apply_it: If you have older children, ask yourself honestly: is there a step toward independence I am holding them back from?

quiz.question: Why did Charles keep his daughters from marrying?
options: No suitable husbands could be found
He said he could not bear to be without their company
They all chose to become nuns
quiz.explanation: He kept them at home because he could not forgo their company, and Einhard admits it led to scandal.

cards.title: The iron-willed king wept openly for his children and his friend
cards.body:
Charles lost two adult sons, Charles and Pippin, and his eldest daughter Rotrude before he died. Einhard, who usually praises his courage, admits the king bore these deaths with less composure than people expected: his love for his family made him weep.

He also wept when Pope Hadrian died in 795, as if he had lost a brother or a dear son. Einhard explains that Charles made friends easily, kept them faithfully and treated them with great respect.

Strength and grief are not opposites. A person can lead armies and still cry for the people they love, and Einhard records it as a mark of his character rather than a weakness.
cards.quote: For he showed a very fine disposition in his friendships: he embraced them readily and maintained them faithfully, and he treated with the utmost respect all whom he had admitted into the circle of his friends.
cards.locator: Part II. Private Life and Character of Charlemagne ¶7
cards.apply_it: Reach out today to one old friend you have let drift, just to say you value them.

quiz.question: How did Charles react to the death of Pope Hadrian?
options: He wept as though he had lost a brother or a dear son
He did not hear about it
quiz.explanation: Einhard says he wept for Hadrian as for a brother or a very dear son.

cards.title: A son left out of the succession was easy prey for plotters
cards.body:
Charles had an elder son, also named Pippin and later called Pippin the Hunchback, born to an earlier partner. Einhard mentions him separately from the other children. When younger sons were given the family names and kingdoms, this Pippin was left outside.

While Charles was wintering in Bavaria early in the Avar war (most historians say 792), some Frankish nobles promised Pippin the throne. He pretended to be ill and joined their plot against his father. It was discovered, the conspirators were punished, and Pippin was sent to the monastery of Prüm, where, Einhard says, he finally took to the religious life of his own will.

A family member who feels excluded is vulnerable to anyone who promises them a place.
cards.quote: this Pippin pretended illness, and formed a conspiracy against his father with some of the leaders of the Franks, who had seduced him by a vain promise of the kingdom.
cards.locator: Part II. Private Life and Character of Charlemagne ¶9
cards.apply_it: Is anyone in your family or team quietly left on the edge? Find one way to bring them in this week.

quiz.question: What drew Pippin the Hunchback into a plot against his father?
options: Nobles who made him an empty promise of the kingdom
quiz.explanation: Einhard says leading Franks seduced him 'by a vain promise of the kingdom'.

cards.title: He drank little and listened to history books over dinner
cards.body:
Einhard describes Charles as moderate in eating and very moderate in drinking: he hated drunkenness, in himself and his friends, and rarely drank more than three times at dinner. He avoided large banquets except on great feast days.

What filled his meals instead was learning. Someone sang or read aloud while he ate, usually histories and the deeds of famous people of the past. He especially loved Saint Augustine's City of God.

Meals are a part of the day most of us already have. Turning even a few of them into time for an audiobook, a podcast or a good conversation is an easy way to keep learning without finding extra hours.
cards.quote: During the meal there was either singing or a reader for him to listen to. Histories and the great deeds of men of old were read to him.
cards.locator: Part II. Private Life and Character of Charlemagne ¶15
cards.apply_it: Pick one meal this week and spend it listening to a chapter of a history book or a thoughtful podcast.

quiz.question: What did Charles listen to while he ate?
options: Histories and the deeds of people of the past, read aloud
quiz.explanation: A reader read histories aloud, and he particularly enjoyed Augustine's City of God.

cards.title: He swam and rode every day, but would not take his doctors' advice
cards.body:
Charles was strong and healthy for most of his life. He rode and hunted constantly, loved the natural hot springs at Aachen, and swam so well that no one could beat him. He often invited his sons, nobles and even his bodyguards to bathe with him.

In his last four years he suffered frequent fevers and became lame in one foot. His doctors told him to give up the roast meat he loved and eat boiled food instead. Einhard says he almost hated them for it and followed his own opinion.

Regular exercise served him well for decades. Ignoring sound advice in later life did not. Good habits do not excuse us from listening when things change.
cards.quote: Even then he followed his own opinion rather than the advice of his doctors, whom he almost hated, because they advised him to give up the roast meat to which he was accustomed, and eat boiled instead.
cards.locator: Part II. Private Life and Character of Charlemagne ¶13
cards.apply_it: Is there health advice you have been brushing off? Write down one small change you could actually try.

quiz.question: What advice from his doctors did Charles refuse to follow?
options: To give up roast meat and eat boiled food instead
quiz.explanation: He loved roast meat and ignored his doctors' advice to switch to boiled food.

cards.title: He spoke Latin as well as his own language, and understood Greek
cards.body:
Charles's native tongue was a Germanic Frankish language, but he did not stop there. Einhard says he took the trouble to learn foreign languages, spoke Latin as fluently as his own language, and could understand Greek better than he could speak it.

He was a ready, clear speaker, so fluent that Einhard admits he sometimes seemed a little talkative.

Latin was the language of the Church, law and learning across Europe, so learning it let a Frankish king deal directly with popes, scholars and foreign courts. A second language still opens doors in the same way, and understanding more than you can speak is a perfectly good place to be.
cards.quote: He was not merely content with his native tongue but took the trouble to learn foreign languages.
cards.locator: Part II. Private Life and Character of Charlemagne ¶18
cards.apply_it: Spend ten minutes today on a language you would like to understand better, even if you never plan to speak it well.

quiz.question: How well did Charles know Greek, according to Einhard?
options: He understood it better than he could speak it
He spoke it better than Latin
quiz.explanation: Einhard says he spoke Latin like his native tongue and understood Greek better than he could speak it.

cards.title: He brought the best teacher in Europe to court, and became his student
cards.body:
Charles honoured teachers. For grammar he studied with Peter of Pisa, an elderly Italian deacon. For everything else his teacher was Alcuin of York, an English scholar who joined the court in 781 and whom Einhard calls the most learned man of his time.

With Alcuin the king studied rhetoric, logic and especially astronomy, and learned arithmetic so he could follow the movement of the stars. Alcuin also ran the palace school, where the children of the court were taught.

Charles had all the power in Europe and still sat down to learn. Finding a real teacher, and being willing to be their student, is a habit worth keeping at any age or rank.
cards.quote: He paid the greatest attention to the liberal arts, and showed the greatest respect and bestowed high honours upon those who taught them.
cards.locator: Part II. Private Life and Character of Charlemagne ¶19
cards.apply_it: Who knows something you would love to learn? Ask them for one hour of teaching this month.

quiz.question: Who was Alcuin?
options: An English scholar from York who taught Charles and led his court's learning
quiz.explanation: Alcuin of York taught Charles rhetoric, logic and astronomy and was, says Einhard, the most learned man of his time.

cards.title: He kept writing tablets under his pillow to practise letters late in life
cards.body:
One of the most human details Einhard gives is this: Charles, already a powerful king, tried to learn to write. He kept tablets and sheets under his pillow so that he could practise forming letters in spare moments, even at night.

He made little progress, Einhard says, because he started too late in life. The editor suggests he could probably write roughly, but never mastered the fine handwriting that trained scribes produced.

What stands out is not the result but the attempt. The most powerful man in Europe was willing to be a beginner, and to keep at it privately. Starting late may limit how far you get, but it is never a reason not to start.
cards.quote: He tried also to learn to write, and for this purpose used to carry with him and keep under the pillow of his couch tablets and writing-sheets that he might in his spare moments accustom himself to the formation of letters.
cards.locator: Part II. Private Life and Character of Charlemagne ¶19
cards.apply_it: What is something you think you are 'too old' to learn? Spend five minutes practising it today.

quiz.question: Why did Charles make little progress in learning to write, according to Einhard?
options: He began too late in life
quiz.explanation: Einhard says the task was begun too late in life, though he kept practising in spare moments.

cards.title: He sent money across the sea to help Christians he would never meet
cards.body:
Einhard says Charles was devoted to almsgiving, gifts to the poor. He gave not only in his own kingdom but sent money across the Mediterranean to Christians in Syria, Egypt, Jerusalem, Alexandria and Carthage whenever he heard of their poverty.

Einhard adds that this was the main reason he cultivated friendships with rulers overseas: he hoped they would ease life for the Christians living under them.

Generosity that reaches beyond your own circle, to people you will never meet, is one of the quieter marks of real faith. It also shows how relationships with the powerful can be used for the good of the vulnerable.
cards.quote: For he gave it his attention not only in his own country and in his own kingdom, but he also used to send money across the sea to Syria, to Egypt, to Africa--to Jerusalem, Alexandria, and Carthage
cards.locator: Part II. Private Life and Character of Charlemagne ¶21
cards.apply_it: Give something this week to a cause that helps people far from where you live.

quiz.question: Why, according to Einhard, did Charles seek friendship with kings overseas?
options: To find wives for his sons
To win help for poor Christians living under their rule
quiz.explanation: Einhard says he cultivated these friendships chiefly to win relief for Christians living under foreign rulers.

cards.title: He divided his treasure in writing so his heirs would not fight
cards.body:
In 811, three years before he died, Charles divided his treasure in front of his bishops, abbots and counts and put the plan in writing. He gave two reasons: that alms would be properly given from his wealth, and that his heirs would know exactly what belonged to them and could share it without dispute.

Most of it went to the twenty-one chief churches of his realm for the poor. Even his large library was to be sold at a fair price and the money given to the poor. A portion went to his children and grandchildren, and a portion to the palace servants.

Clear written wishes are a kindness to the people you leave behind.
cards.quote: and also that his heirs may clearly know without any possibility of doubt what ought to belong to them, and may therefore (without contest or dissension) divide his goods among themselves in their proper proportion.
cards.locator: Part II. Private Life and Character of Charlemagne ¶33
cards.apply_it: If you have no will or written wishes, set a date this month to start one.

quiz.question: What was one main purpose of Charles's written division of his treasure?
options: To hide money from the Pope
So his heirs could divide his goods without dispute
To pay for a new war
To give everything to his eldest son
quiz.explanation: He wanted his heirs to know clearly what belonged to them, so they could share it without quarrel.

cards.title: He named his heir with the nobles' consent, then died at Aachen in 814
cards.body:
In 813, feeling old and ill, Charles called his only surviving son by Hildegard, Louis, king of Aquitaine, to Aachen, assembled the Frankish nobles and, with their agreement, made Louis co-emperor and heir. The decision was welcomed, and the handover was settled before any crisis.

That autumn he still went hunting. In winter he caught a fever and, as was his habit, tried to cure it by fasting. Pleurisy followed, and on 28 January 814, in his seventy-second year and the forty-seventh of his reign, he died. He was buried the same day in the church he had built at Aachen.

Settling succession while you still can is one of a leader's last and most important tasks.
cards.quote: and then, with the consent of all, made Lewis partner in the whole kingdom and heir to the imperial title.
cards.locator: Part II. Private Life and Character of Charlemagne ¶27
cards.apply_it: If you lead anything, who could take over tomorrow? Share one key piece of knowledge with them this week.

quiz.question: How did Charles arrange his succession?
options: He left it to the Pope
He named Louis co-emperor with the consent of the nobles
He divided the empire among all his grandsons
He made no plan at all
quiz.explanation: In 813 he made Louis his partner and heir, with the agreement of the assembled Frankish nobles.

cards.title: Seventy years after his death, Charlemagne was already turning into legend
cards.body:
The second half of this book is a collection of stories written around 883 by a monk of the abbey of St Gall, in what is now Switzerland. Many scholars identify him as Notker the Stammerer, though the editor thought his name could not be known for sure. He wrote for the emperor Charles the Fat, using tales from old soldiers and clerics.

The editor warns that the Monk's account is full of legend, invention and mistakes: wrong popes, wrong queens, miracles performed on Charles's behalf. Einhard wrote as an eyewitness; the Monk wrote as a storyteller with a moral to teach.

The stories in the next cards are legends, not reliable history. They are worth reading for what people came to believe about Charles, which is its own kind of truth.
cards.quote: The restrained, positive, well-arranged narrative of Eginhard seems to belong to a different age from the garrulous, credulous, and hopelessly jumbled story of the Monk of Saint Gall.
cards.locator: Introduction ¶1
cards.apply_it: When you hear a great story about a famous person, ask: who first told it, and how long after the events?

quiz.question: How does the editor describe the Monk of St Gall's account?
options: As the most reliable source on Charlemagne
As full of legend and mistakes, unlike Einhard's restrained narrative
quiz.explanation: He contrasts Einhard's careful narrative with the Monk's 'garrulous, credulous, and hopelessly jumbled' story.

cards.title: 'Wisdom for sale': the legend of the two Irish teachers
cards.body:
The Monk tells a story, legendary but charming, of two Irish scholars who landed in Gaul with some British merchants. At the market they offered no goods. Instead they called out that they had wisdom for sale, because people only valued what they had to pay for.

When Charles summoned them and asked the price, they said they wanted no money: only a place to teach, eager minds, and food and clothing. Delighted, he gave one of them a school and sent him boys of every rank, and sent the other to teach at Pavia in Italy.

The best teachers ask for very little: a place, willing students and enough to live on. Supporting them is one of the best investments a community can make.
cards.quote: We ask no price, O king; but we ask only for a fit place for teaching and quick minds to teach; and besides food to eat and raiment to put on, for without these we cannot accomplish our pilgrimage.
cards.locator: Book I. Concerning the Piety of Charles and His Care of the Church ¶2
cards.apply_it: Thank a teacher who shaped you, or find a small way to support a teacher today.

quiz.question: What price did the two scholars ask for their wisdom, in the Monk's story?
options: Only a place to teach, eager students, and food and clothing
quiz.explanation: They asked no money, only a place to teach, quick minds and the basics of life.

cards.title: In the palace school, the poor boys' hard work beat the nobles' birth
cards.body:
In another of the Monk's stories, Charles returned from a long campaign and asked the boys at his school to show him their writing. The sons of poor and middle-class families had done excellent work. The sons of nobles had produced, the Monk says, silly and tasteless pieces.

Charles put the hardworking boys on his right and promised them bishoprics and abbeys if they kept studying. To the nobles' sons he said that their birth and good looks meant nothing to him, and that unless they made up for their laziness they would never get his favour.

The tale may be embellished, but its point holds: effort, not background, is what earns real trust.
cards.quote: By the King of Heaven, I take no account of your noble birth and your fine looks, though others may admire you for them.
cards.locator: Book I. Concerning the Piety of Charles and His Care of the Church ¶5
cards.apply_it: When you next judge someone's work, look only at the work. Notice if their background was quietly influencing you.

quiz.question: In the Monk's story, which boys did Charles praise?
options: The boys of middle or humble birth who worked hard
quiz.explanation: He praised the poorer boys for their excellent work and rebuked the nobles' sons for relying on birth.

cards.title: Alcuin told the king his expectations were too high, and got away with it
cards.body:
The Monk tells how Charles, pleased with the spread of learning but still unsatisfied, once sighed: if only he had twelve clergy as learned as Saint Jerome and Saint Augustine, two of the greatest scholars of the early Church.

Alcuin, who felt small beside those names, replied with a boldness, the Monk says, that no one else dared before the formidable king: the Creator himself had few men like those, and Charles expected twelve?

Even if embellished, the story captures something true about their friendship. Good advisers tell a leader when a demand is unrealistic, and good leaders keep such advisers close.
cards.quote: The Maker of heaven and earth has not many like to those men and do you expect to have twelve?
cards.locator: Book I. Concerning the Piety of Charles and His Care of the Church ¶18
cards.apply_it: Is someone asking more of you or your team than is realistic? Say so, clearly and respectfully.

quiz.question: What did Charles wish for, prompting Alcuin's bold reply?
options: Twelve clergy as learned as Jerome and Augustine
quiz.explanation: Alcuin answered that God himself had few such men, so twelve was too much to expect.

cards.title: Accused of breaking his fast, he showed the bishop who was really waiting
cards.body:
In the Monk's telling, Charles took his Lent meal in the early afternoon, earlier than strict custom. A bishop rebuked him for it. Charles accepted the rebuke politely and then gave the bishop some advice of his own: do not eat until the humblest servant at court has been fed.

The bishop obeyed. Because the court ate in rank order, kings and dukes first, servants last, the lowest servants did not eat until midnight. By the end of Lent the bishop understood: Charles ate early not from weakness, but so that everyone below him could eat at a decent hour.

Leaders' habits often have reasons that are invisible from outside. Before criticising, ask who else is affected.
cards.quote: Now, sir bishop, I think you have found out that it is not lack of self-restraint but care for others which makes me dine in Lent before the hour of evening.
cards.locator: Book I. Concerning the Piety of Charles and His Care of the Church ¶22
cards.apply_it: Before criticising someone's routine this week, ask them why they do it that way.

quiz.question: Why did Charles eat early during Lent, according to the Monk?
options: So that those who ate after him, down to the lowest servants, were not kept waiting until midnight
quiz.explanation: The court ate in order of rank, so his early meal let everyone below him eat at a reasonable hour.

cards.title: When a nervous clerk faked his singing, the emperor thanked him
cards.body:
The Monk tells of a wandering clerk who wandered into the royal choir without knowing its strict rules. Threatened by the choirmaster's staff, he could only pretend, twisting his neck and puffing his cheeks to look like he was singing. Everyone laughed.

Charles seemed not to notice and waited calmly until the service ended. Then he called the frightened man over, thanked him for his singing and his effort, and gave him a pound of silver to ease his poverty.

When someone is struggling and exposed, the kind response is to protect their dignity, not add to the laughter. A few gentle words from the person in charge can turn humiliation into gratitude.
cards.quote: Many thanks, good clerk, for your singing and your efforts.
cards.locator: Book I. Concerning the Piety of Charles and His Care of the Church ¶16
cards.apply_it: Next time someone stumbles in public, find one sincere thing to thank them for.

quiz.question: How did Charles respond to the clerk who could only pretend to sing?
options: He thanked him for his effort and gave him silver
quiz.explanation: He ignored the mockery, thanked the clerk for his efforts and gave him money to relieve his poverty.

cards.title: In legend, he wept at the sight of Viking ships, foreseeing his heirs' troubles
cards.body:
The Monk tells that Charles was once dining in a harbour town in southern France when raiders' ships appeared. Others took them for merchants, but Charles recognised them as Northmen. The raiders fled on hearing he was there.

Charles then stood at a window weeping for a long time. He explained that he did not fear these raiders for himself. He grieved because they had dared to touch his coast while he lived, and he foresaw what they would do to his descendants.

The story is legend, written after Viking raids had indeed torn at his weakened empire. Its lesson is real: a leader's work is measured partly by what survives after they are gone.
cards.quote: I have no fear of those worthless rascals doing any harm to me; but I am sad at heart to think that even during my lifetime they have dared to touch this shore
cards.locator: Book II. Concerning the Wars and Military Exploits of Charles ¶38
cards.apply_it: Think about something you are building. What would it need to survive without you?

quiz.question: Why did Charles weep in the Monk's story about the Viking ships?
options: He was afraid for his own life
He foresaw the harm they would do to his descendants
The ships carried bad news from Rome
quiz.explanation: He feared not for himself but for his heirs and their subjects, a fear later Viking raids made real.
